The FD&C Act requires that a brand owner of a face serum made by a contract lab ensure and maintain records supporting adequate substantiation of safety of the product before and while marketing it. This includes maintaining evidence that the product is safe under the conditions of use prescribed in the labeling or customary/usual conditions, where "safe" means not injurious to users, and minor transient reactions do not constitute injury. The requirement for adequate substantiation of safety involves tests, studies, research, analyses, or other evidence considered sufficient by experts qualified by scientific training and experience to evaluate the safety of cosmetic products and their ingredients. The requirement may consider cumulative or relevant exposure to the product or ingredient when determining safety. 

FD&C Act § 608(a) [21 U.S.C. 364d(a)] requires a responsible person for a cosmetic product to ensure and maintain records supporting adequate substantiation of safety of such product.  
FD&C Act § 608(c)(1) [21 U.S.C. 364d(c)(1)] defines "adequate substantiation of safety" as tests or studies, research, analyses, or other evidence considered sufficient by experts qualified by scientific training and experience to evaluate the safety of cosmetic products and their ingredients.  
FD&C Act § 608(c)(2) [21 U.S.C. 364d(c)(2)] defines "safe" as meaning the product is not injurious under the conditions of use prescribed in labeling or customary/usual conditions, and the Secretary shall not consider a cosmetic ingredient or product injurious solely because it causes minor and transient reactions or irritations in some users.  
FD&C Act § 608(c)(3) [21 U.S.C. 364d(c)] allows consideration of cumulative or other relevant exposure to the cosmetic product, including any ingredient, when determining whether a product is safe.  

The requirement does not apply to coal-tar hair dye if it otherwise complies with section 361(a), as specified in FD&C Act § 608(b) [21 U.S.C. 364d(b)].  
The responsible person for the face serum, defined as the manufacturer, packer, or distributor whose name appears on the label, is required to maintain records supporting safety substantiation, per FD&C Act § 604(4) [21 U.S.C. 364(4)].
